one_liner: Snap's maintained Djinni IDL bridge generator (C++ to Java/JNI, Objective-C, WASM/TypeScript); claims 5-10x faster JNI string passing than Dropbox's original.
what_it_does: You describe records, enums and interfaces in a .djinni IDL file; a Scala code generator emits C++ headers plus JNI, Objective-C++ and Embind/TypeScript glue, and a small support library (support-lib/) does the marshalling at run time. It continues the archived dropbox/djinni and adds array<>, outcome<>, future<>, Protobuf types, DataView/DataRef zero-copy buffers and WASM output. It is a different tool from a serializer: you call C++ objects from Java/Kotlin, Swift/ObjC or JS, and the generated glue converts arguments on each call.
how_it_is_fast: The string speedup comes from replacing Dropbox's per-code-point miniutf transcoding (a validating decode and an initializer-list append for every code point) with bulk std::wstring_convert<std::codecvt_utf8_utf16<char16_t>> conversion from the platform C++ library, followed by one NewString call. Separately, array<T> marshals primitive element types through GetPrimitiveArrayCritical and a single copy into a Java T[], where list<T> boxes each element through a Long.valueOf JNI call; DataView/DataRef expose direct ByteBuffers via GetDirectBufferAddress instead of copying.
when_to_use: Mobile apps sharing one C++ core across Android (JNI), iOS (ObjC/Swift) and the web (WASM), where hand-written JNI glue is the alternative.
Projects still on archived dropbox/djinni that pass strings across the JNI boundary often and want the cheaper conversion plus bug fixes.

Interfaces that move primitive vectors: declare them array<i32/i64/f64> instead of list<> to avoid per-element boxing (perftest example: argArrayInt 128 at 8,210 ns versus argListInt 128 at 353,718 ns, about 43x, derived from page data).
Large binary payloads that should not be copied per call: use DataView (borrowed direct ByteBuffer/NSData) or DataRef (owned, can steal a std::vector<uint8_t> or std::string buffer).
when_not_to_use: Strings that may carry invalid UTF-8 from C++ or unpaired surrogates from Java (for example a Java String cut in the middle of an emoji): the fork throws std::range_error where Dropbox substituted U+FFFD; the maintainer calls this intentional (issue #86) and points to binary/DataView/DataRef for non-text data.

Builds that must move to C++26 or treat deprecation warnings as errors: the string path relies on std::wstring_convert/std::codecvt_utf8_utf16 (deprecated in C++17, removed in C++26); issue #199 reports 14 -Wdeprecated-declarations warnings on Android with C++20 on main.
Teams that cannot install Bazel and a JVM: the code generator is built and run through Bazel (README FAQ), even though generated files can go into any build system.
Apps with very many live interface objects on Android: each interface object crossing JNI holds one JNI global reference, and the README warns the limit is usually about 64k.
If you need a measured, reproducible speedup: the 5-10x string claim has no published before/after benchmark, and the bundled perftest only times the fork itself.

integration.form: source-drop (generated C++/JNI/ObjC++/WASM sources plus support-lib sources compiled into your app); the generator is a Scala binary built with Bazel
integration.dependencies: Bazel and a JVM to build/run the generator; at run time JNI (Android/JVM), the Objective-C runtime (Apple), or Emscripten Embind (WASM); optional Protobuf for protobuf types
integration.min_toolchain: main branch: C++17 (.bazelrc passes -std=c++17; README pins Android SDK 30.0.2 and NDK 21.4.7075529 for the examples). experimental-record branch (the one Snap uses): C++20, Bazel 8.5.0+, Java 8+
integration.platforms: Android and desktop JVM via JNI, iOS/macOS via Objective-C (Swift and C API backends on experimental-record per open PR #225), browsers via WASM/TypeScript
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the fork README
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the IDL is a superset of dropbox/djinni and output must be regenerated; generated code differs (CppProxy finalizers removed, invalid UTF now throws, and on experimental-record records become mutable with optionals omitted from constructors unless --*-legacy-records is passed)

gotchas: Code-read finding: jniUTF8FromString and jniWStringFromString (support-lib/jni/djinni_support.cpp on main and experimental-record) call GetStringChars without a null check and release it with a plain ReleaseStringChars after the conversion, not through an RAII guard; when Utf8Converter::to_bytes throws std::range_error on a lone surrogate, ReleaseStringChars is skipped and the chars buffer is leaked or left pinned. Dropbox's original used a unique_ptr deleter. (Inferred from the code, not tested.)

Perftest harness flaw: MainActivity.kt builds its test strings with Kotlin inclusive ranges (for i in 0..lowCount/minCount), so the rows labelled argString 128/4096/16384 actually pass 144, 4,752 and 23,760 characters; all strings are ASCII ('1234567890ABCDEF' and '@'), the best case for UTF transcoding; there is no warm-up and each row averages 1,000 single-call nanoTime samples including outliers (row maxima up to 5.3 ms; returnString 16384 max 1.92 ms). The rows labelled argArrayRecord/returnArrayRecord are declared list<RecordSixInt> in djinni_perf_benchmark.djinni, so they measure list<>.

The perftest build documents no optimization level: README says 'bazel build perftest', and neither .bazelrc nor perftest/BUILD or support-lib/BUILD sets -c opt or -O flags, so the example output may come from Bazel's default fastbuild mode (not stated). That would also favor a precompiled libc++ codecvt over inline hand-written code in any before/after comparison.

Two live lines: main has had no commit since 2024-10-28, while Snap develops on experimental-record (commits to 2026-10-09; open PR #225 merges 224 commits into main), which changes record semantics and raises the toolchain to C++20/Bazel 8.5.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings in this category (Cista++, struct_pack, bitsery, YAS, FBE, the enum-reflection libraries) generates cross-language call bindings; pick Djinni when the bottleneck is calling C++ from Java/Kotlin, ObjC/Swift or JS, and pair it with one of those serializers over DataView/DataRef if you need to move structured data in bulk rather than per-field.
verified_claims_summary: The only performance evidence is the fork README's one-line, first-party claim that string passing between Java and C++ is about 5-10x faster than Dropbox's handwritten conversion, with no device, string sizes, Android/NDK version or compiler flags. The repo's Android perftest prints absolute timings for the fork only (for example argString 16 chars at 4,622 ns and the row labelled 16384, really 23,760 ASCII chars, at 109,606 ns; returnString 16,384 chars at 230,499 ns), on an unnamed device and build mode; a search snippet of Snap's 2021 'Improving Djinni' post mentions string marshalling gains (a newsletter summary says 3-10x) but the post (eng.snap.com) is blocked here.
status_note: Apache-2.0 and copyable; the record's 'stale' status reflects only the main branch (last commit 2024-10-28): Snap actively maintains the experimental-record branch (commits through 2026-10-09, merge PR #225 open since 2026-10-08), so treat the project as active but expect a C++20/Bazel 8.5 jump and record-semantics changes when that branch lands.
